abstract_text: The family Rhombosoleidae is composed of nine genera distributed in Australia, New Zealand and South America. We have examined the phylogenetic status of two genera: the Indo-Pacific Psammodiscus and the South American Oncopterus. The former genus shows a caudal skeleton that is typical of what is observed in the Samaridae while the latter has a series of secondary canals perpendicular to the lateral line which resembles the series found in the South American achirines (Achiridae). A complete osteological survey of all rhombosoleid species and outgroups combined with a review of the morphological characters used in past studies will be used to clarify the phylogenetic status of these two genera and examine the monophyletic status of the family Rhombosoleidae.

title: Effects of the presence of fish on the suitability of breeding sites to Ambystoma maculatum

authors.affiliation: University of Guelph, Guelph, ON, N1G 2W1, Canada
University of Guelph, Guelph, ON, N1G 2W1, Canada

abstract_text: The presence of predatory fish is thought to restrict successful breeding by many amphibians, including Ambystoma maculatum (the spotted salamander), to temporary ponds. Evidence is accumulating, however, that A. maculatum sometimes breeds successfully in the presence of fish. I investigated the co-occurrence of breeding A. maculatum and fish in 11 lakes in Algonquin Park, Ontario. Stepwise multiple regression was used to determine the relative importance of the effects of the presence/absence of fish, pH, Secchi depth, lake area, and the forest type surrounding the lakes on the density of egg masses in lakes. Variation in egg mass density among the lakes was significantly related to the presence/absence of fish (excluding Salvelinus fontinalis), but was not related to any of the other habitat variables. The larvae were palatable to fishes, but larvae successfully reached metamorphosis in at least one lake despite the presence of fish. Although presence of fish was the most important factor in the suitability of a breeding site to A. maculatum, fish did not completely exclude A. maculatum. The use of refuges, spatially complex habitats, and a bet-hedging life history, are potential ways in which A. maculatum can reproduce despite the presence of fish.

title: Diel activity patterns of the sympatric Poison Dart frogs Dendrobates auratus and D. pumilio in Costa Rica

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Northern Michigan University, Marquette, MI 49855, USA

abstract_text: Activity of Dendrobates auratus and D. pumilio in Northeastern Costa Rica was monitored at 45 min intervals throughout daylight hours on nine days in late-June and early-July 1997. Activity of D. pumilio peaked early in the morning, declined steadily to mid-day, then remained at relatively low levels through the afternoon. Activity of D. auratus peaked later in the day, and was more consistent throughout the day than was activity of D. pumilio. Dendrobates auratus was usually found on the ground, and no association was found between percent of individuals on elevated perches and observation time. In contrast, there was a clear peak in use of elevated perches by D. pumilio which occurred shortly after sunrise. A significant positive relationship between rainfall and activity was evident for D. pumilio, but not for D. auratus. These data demonstrate differences in activity patterns between these congeners, in spite of many ecological similarities.

title: A telemetric study of the home ranges and movement patterns of the mountain yellow-legged frog Rana muscosa in Dusy Basin, Kings Canyon National Park

abstract_text: Rana muscosa was once common throughout high elevation areas of the Sierra Nevada but has declined primarily due to widespread stocking of non-native trout. To understand Rana muscosa habitat needs, we initiated a telemetric study in 1997 to determine home ranges and movement patterns during the summer and fall when their high elevation habitats (>3000 m) are accessible. We used radio transmitters and GPS to map the locations of 24 frogs in Dusy Basin. During the summer frogs were distributed throughout the basin in a variety of lakes. In August 12 tagged frogs showed no movement away from the small lakes where they were originally captured and tagged, and their home ranges were small (within 50 m). In September 8 of 9 frogs moved up to 200 m away from their original capture lakes. By October, when lakes began freezing, frogs were found in only two lakes along the shoreline in deep crevices or under rock ledges. This initial telemetry study of Rana muscosa indicates they are more widely distributed during the summer, and become more restricted in their distribution as the lakes freeze. Future restoration strategies should ensure their access to their summer and winter habitats.

title: Mountain yellow-legged frog habitat use and movement patterns in a high elevation basin in Kings Canyon National Park: a mark-recapture study

abstract_text: We are studying the movement patterns of Rana muscosa to determine seasonal habitat use related to hibernation, breeding activity and feeding. Passive integrated transponders (PIT tags) were inserted into 471 adult frogs in Dusy Basin, Kings Canyon National Park (elevation 3470m) during the summer of 1997. Recapture surveys were conducted between August and October when the activity cycle ended and lakes began to freeze. Throughout August all recaptured frogs remained in the same water body where they were originally tagged. Frogs were observed feeding and sunning in daylight hours during this period. By mid September, a high percentage of frogs were recaptured in different water bodies than where they were originally tagged. Frogs moved from the 12 water bodies they were found during the summer feeding period to only 2 lakes in the basin. One of the lakes was small and shallow (<.2 ha, <2 m deep) while the other was the largest lake in the basin (4.3 ha, 9 m deep). Above-water activity greatly declined after this movement period. This study will be continued in 1998 to gain information about movement between overwintering habitats and breeding sites and movement between breeding and feeding sites. Because Rana muscosa has declined throughout the Sierra Nevada, understanding their habitat requirements will be crucial in managing remaining populations.

abstract_text: We summarize preliminary results of the mid-point data collection for a large-scale, long-term field study of herp communities and the influence of habitat and landscape environmental variables in the Ouachita Mountains of west-central Arkansas, USA. This study is one component of Phase III of the Ouachita Mountains Ecosystem Management Research Project and is a cooperative effort involving the Ouachita National Forest, Weyerhaeuser Company, the National Council of the Paper Industry for Air and Stream Improvement, Oklahoma State University, the Oklahoma Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, the University of Arkansas Monticello, and the Southern Forest Experiment Station of the National Forest Service. The primary objective is to strengthen our knowledge of habitat relationships of amphibians and reptiles at both the stand and landscape level using four 1500 to 3800 ha watersheds with different histories of silviculture and intensity of timber management. Thus far, the most intensively managed watershed is lower in diversity per plot (alpha-diversity) for both amphibians and reptiles, whereas ordination indicates that this watershed is greater in diversity among plots (beta-diversity) for both taxa.

title: Use of discarded aluminum beverage cans by selected North American amphibians and reptiles

authors.affiliation: U.S. Geological Survey, Biological Resources Division, 39913 Sharon Avenue, Davis, CA 95616, USA; Research Associate, Dept. of Herpetology, California Academy of Sciences, Golden Gate Park, San Francisco, CA 94118, USA

abstract_text: Over the past 35 years, discarded aluminum beverage cans have become a common item of litter in many parts of North America. Although the shape, volume, and opening of these cans have changed many times over the years, their use as shelter by selected invertebrates, fishes, amphibians, reptiles, and small mammals indicates that these anthropogenic items may provide suitable hiding places in otherwise desolate habitats. Over the past 2 years, I have collected over 10,000 discarded aluminum beverage cans under a wide variety of conditions in California, Nevada, Oregon, and Washington. Although a significant number of cans contained dead invertebrates, most were found to be devoid of amphibians and reptiles. However, a small number of cans were found to house Pacific treefrogs (Hyla regilla), southern alligator lizards (Elgaria multicarinata), western skinks (Eumeces skiltonianus), western fence lizards (Sceloporus occidentalis), and side-blotched lizards (Uta stansburiana). Some of the lizards observed in these cans were found to be in various stages of decomposition. The individual preferences of amphibians and reptiles for selected beer and soft drink cans will be discussed.

abstract_text: There has recently been concern that amphibians are declining in abundance and diversity on a global scale. Since 1985, the population dynamics of three species of Ranid amphibians (Rana catesbeiana, Rana clamitans and Rana septentrionalis) have been investigated using intensive mark-recapture techniques. The focus of this long-term study is to test whether these species are experiencing declines in the relatively pristine environment of the Wildlife Research Area of Algonquin Provincial Park, Ontario. To date, the study indicates that population sizes of all three species of Ranids fluctuate from year to year. However, there is no evidence of significant decreases in abundance or mean body size, or of shifts in the age distribution over the 10-year sampling period. This suggests that over the time scale of our study, broad environmental factors such as increased ultraviolet radiation or global warming, are not important determinants of amphibian abundance in this region.

title: Overwintering habitats of radio-implanted green frogs, Rana clamitans

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Binghamton, N.Y. 13902-6000, USA
Department of Biological Sciences, Binghamton, N.Y. 13902-6000, USA

abstract_text: Winter's freezing temperatures exert a major selective force on temperate frogs and toads. The selection of an overwintering site that provides protection from freezing is critical for those species without freeze tolerance. Many freeze intolerant frogs, such as the green frog (Rana clamitans), are commonly assumed to overwinter at the bottom of shallow, eutrophic, breeding ponds. Although anurans overwintering in pond bottoms would avoid freezing, these environments are highly anoxic for the majority of winter. Since adult ranids cannot tolerate anoxia for even limited periods of time, it is unlikely that pond bottoms would be suitable overwintering sites. Anurans may need to undergo extensive movements in search of suitable overwintering sites that remain unfrozen and provide adequate oxygen for survival. We used radio implants to determine overwintering habitats of the green frog in southern New York state. In late fall, green frogs moved 80-480 m from their summer breeding ponds to streams and seeps that remained flowing and unfrozen throughout winter. We suggest that these sites are chosen because they remain unfrozen and remain well oxygenated.

title: How venom-conducting fangs are formed

authors.affiliation: Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, U.S.A.

abstract_text: Venom-delivery systems occur in at least four families of snakes. In viperids, elapids, and atractaspidids, the venom-delivery system is front-fanged, and consists of a hollow fang and a venom gland associated with compressor muscles, which squeeze venom into a duct, which carries it to the proximal end of the fang, where it enters the venom canal. In venomous colubrids the fang is grooved rather than hollow, and positioned at the posterior end of the maxilla. It is not known how many times the venom-delivery system has been independently derived in snakes. This study was initially undertaken to determine how venom-conducting fangs form during development in different groups of snakes, in the hope that this might shed light on the question of how venom-conducting fangs were arrived at evolutionarily. It was found that published descriptions of fang formation in snakes disagree about how fangs are formed. This disagreement is discussed along with developmental differences between fangs in embryonic snakes and replacement fangs in adult snakes, and their implications for reconstructing the evolutionary history of snakes.

title: Application of a modified index of biotic integrity to detect changes in fish assemblages in a historically degraded river system

authors.affiliation: The University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996, USA

abstract_text: The New River, a tributary of the Big South Fork of the Cumberland River in northeast Tennessee, has been degraded by siltation associated with coal mine drainage. Electrofishing samples from 42 localities in 1996 revealed recent increases in the range of intolerant species and the return of extirpated fishes to the river system. A modified index of biotic integrity (IBI), relative to the New River, was compiled using components of fish assemblages (metrics) that reflect the impacts of siltation. Replicate fish samples were obtained by using a bootstrap resampling algorithm that enabled tests for significant differences among IBI scores. Comparisons of IBI scores from 13 electrofishing samples completed in 1977 and repeated during 1996 indicate that the health of fish assemblages and water quality have improved during the past two decades.

title: Cryptic though not concealed: phylogenetic relationships of Asian leaf-litter frogs revealed through mitochondrial DNA sequences (Anura: Megophryidae)

authors.affiliation: Royal Ontario Museum, Centre for Biodiversity and Conservation Biology, 100 Queen's Park, Toronto, Ontario, M1E 4W9, Canada

abstract_text: The family Megophryidae is distributed throughout Southeast Asia and includes more than 85 species among its seven genera. At present, there is virtually nothing known about the inter-generic relationships of the family. Some ideas have been put forth for some of the genera or for the group as a whole, but these hypotheses have been largely based on intuition, and not supported by a phylogenetic analysis. I will discuss the results of a phylogenetic analysis of DNA sequences from 21 species, representing 6 of the 7 genera of Megophryidae. The parsimony analysis was performed using 1624 base pairs from mitochondrial genes 12S and 16S in which 650 sites were informative. The data from the two genes were analyzed separately and in a combined analysis. The results from the two data sets are highly congruent. There is strong support for the subfamily Leptobrachiinae (Dubois) and Megophryinae (Noble) as has been suggested from morphological data. Patterns of relationships within these subfamilies will be discussed.

title: A description of flight in the flying snake, Chrysopelea paradisi

authors.affiliation: Department of Organismal Biology and Anatomy, University of Chicago, 1027 East 57th St., Chicago, IL 60637, USA

abstract_text: Passive (gliding) flight has been studied in some vertebrate fliers, but is essentially unexplored in the flying snakes of the genus Chrysopelea. Four specimens of Chrysopelea paradisi were videotaped in flight from a height of 11 meters. Seventy-five total flights were recorded. For comparison, locomotion of the snake in water and on land were also recorded. Chrysopelea is capable of beginning its flight either in mid-air or from a controlled launch. In a launch, the body is coiled back against the substrate, then sprung forward horizontally. By the end of the launch, the body is flattened dorsoventrally from head to vent. In flight the snake undulates laterally in a swimming-like motion with the body in a plane parallel with the ground. The amplitude of undulation in air is more than twice that of undulation in water. Over the course of a flight, the frequency of undulation decreases. Upon landing, the snake contacts the ground tail first, then body, and head last. The snake is capable of extensive maneuvering in flight, able to turn ninety degrees within a meter. Video clips of the flight will be shown.

title: Phylogenetic relationships of the Kinosternon flavescens species group inferred from complete mitochondrial control region sequences

authors.affiliation: Illinois Natural History Survey, 607 E. Peabody Drive, Champaign, IL 61820, USA

abstract_text: Subspecific designations within the wide ranging yellow mud turtle, Kinosternon flavescens, have been controversial. Identification of the four subspecies of K. flavescens (K. f. flavescens, K. f. arizonense, K. f. durangoense, and K. f. spooneri), have been based on nondiscrete morphological characters and biogeography. Three previous phenetic studies of the K. flavescens species group, using morphometric characters, resulted in conflicting taxonomic conclusions. In order to assess evolutionary relationships among populations of K. flavescens, complete gene sequences (1100 base pairs) of the mitochondrial control region were analyzed using parsimony, maximum likelihood, and distance methods. Historical biogeographic patterns, inferred from the generated phylogeny, were used to test hypotheses of climatic change during the Pleistocene (e.g. the Prairie Peninsula region). The structure and evolution of the control region in Kinosternid turtles was characterized and compared to other vertebrate taxa, including fish, birds, and mammals.

title: Diet overlap and parasite assemblage structure in Atchafalaya River Basin fishes

authors.affiliation: School of Forestry Wildlife and Fisheries, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, 70803, USA

abstract_text: We collected adults of seven fish species from lake, canal, and flooded swamp sites to determine trophic overlap and factors structuring parasite assemblages. White bass, Morone chrysops, are specialists for normoxic (Dissolved Oxygen >4 mg) lake and riverine habitats while warmouth Lepomis gulosus, spotted gar Lepisosteus occulatus and bowfin, Amia calva, are hypoxic (D.O. <2 mg) water specialists preferring bayous and swamps. Crappies, Pomoxis nigromaculatus and P. annularis and largemouth bass, Micropterus salmoides, are considered to be generalists for habitat and feeding guilds. Bluegill, L. macrochirus, was considered an invertivore habitat generalist. Fish diets and trophically transmitted parasites were examined to determine diet similarity among species and the importance of host phylogeny, diet and habitat in structuring parasite assemblages. Host ecology was a more important determinant of parasite assemblages than phylogeny, and parasite distributions indicated some resource partitioning among fishes examined. Generalist parasites did not occur in all host species they are known to infect. These results suggest fine scale resource partitioning within fish trophic guilds and stronger partitioning by habitat preference.

title: Evolutionary endocrinology of accelerated metamorphosis in spadefoot toads

authors.affiliation: Department of Integrative Biology, Museum of Vertebrate Zoology, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA
Department of Integrative Biology, Museum of Vertebrate Zoology, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA

abstract_text: Spadefoot species in Scaphiopus and Spea have short larval periods compared to their closest relatives in Pelobates. We examined two potential explanations for differences in length of the larval period between genera. First, histological examination of thyroid gland development in representatives of all spadefoot genera, Scaphiopus couchii, Spea multiplicata, and Pelobates syriacus, showed that colloid appeared earlier in Sp. multiplicata and later in Sc. couchii compared to Pb. syriacus, suggesting differences in differentiation of the thyroid axis. Second, tissue sensitivity and responsivity to thyroid hormone was examined using an in vitro tail tip assay, where tail shrinkage was measured in response to exogenous thyroid hormone. Total area and perimeter of four tail tips in each of six thyroid hormone concentrations (0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 nM) at three developmental stages (Gosner stages 28, 33, and 37) per species (Sc. couchii, Sp. multiplicata, and Pb. syriacus) were measured daily for fourteen days. Sc. couchii tails shrank in response to 2-8 nM tri-iodothyronine, compared to 4-8 nM for Sp. multiplicata and Pb. syriacus tails. At 4 and 8 nM, Sc. couchii and Sp. multiplicata tails shrank faster than P. syriacus tails. Scaphiopus and Spea may have achieved higher metamorphic rates from increased responsivity to thyroid hormone, and Scaphiopus may have improved upon this mechanism by increasing its sensitivity to thyroid hormone.

title: Tale of two puffers: Do motor patterns change with a shift in muscle insertion?

abstract_text: Durophagous fishes of the order Tetraodontiformes use stalwart teeth and jaws to process prey. Idiosyncratic in their reliance on oral manipulation and crushing during feeding, they possess a relatively complex adductor mandibulae musculature as compared to those fishes of the ancestral, pharyngeal jaw-processing persuasion. A1 and A2 adductor mandibulae muscles orchestrate the closing and biting forces. Dog-faced pufferfishes in the genus Arothron possess a plesiomorphic insertion of the A2 muscle on the lower jaw. Southern puffers of the genus Sphoeroides, in contrast, have a novel shift in A2 insertion from the dentary to the maxilla. Lack of linkage between anatomical change and subsequent functional consequence serves to reinforce motor pattern conservation during muscle evolution. Electromyographic recordings of jaw muscles from both genera were taken as puffers fed on prey of varying texture (fiddler crabs and shrimp). Quantified with EMG variables including burst duration, relative onset and intensity, motor pattern differences were manifest only in an across-the-board earlier onset of adductor firing in Southern puffers.

abstract_text: When studying snake reproductive ecology, offspring characteristics are one of the most difficult reproductive traits to quantify in a natural setting. title: A field population of bullfrog tadpoles with a highly female-biased sex ratio

abstract_text: The timing of the occurrence of sex differentiation is variable among anuran amphibians. While some frog species exhibit sexual differentiation after metamorphosis, others differentiate during the larval period. In order to determine the timing of sexual differentiation in the bullfrog, Rana catesbeiana, we collected 82 tadpoles from a fish hatchery in northern Arizona. Upon histological examination we found that differentiation was evident by Gosner Stage 35. Furthermore, among differentiated animals, 88.6% of the population was female, with only 11.5% of the population being male. Two of the male specimens had poorly organized seminiferous tubules with oocytes embedded within the testicular tissue. One female had a polynuclear oocyte. We cannot say what may have affected this population of bullfrog tadpoles, but our histological results suggest that these animals may have been exposed to some form of xenobiotic contamination.

title: The effects of xenobiotics on larval development in the bullfrog (Rana catesbeiana)

abstract_text: Xenobiotic compounds have been hypothesized to disrupt normal growth and development and induce gross morphological mutations and abnormalities. Embryonic exposure to endocrine disrupting compounds may alter the formation of endocrine tissues, leading to abnormalities in the timing or outcome of the sexual differentiation of gonadal tissue. Previous research demonstrated the occurrence of gonadal abnormalities in juvenile alligators collected from a contaminated lake site (Guillette, Crain, and Rooney, 1997). In a study examining the developmental timing of sexual differentiation of Rana catesbeiana from a local fish hatchery, we were surprised to find a highly skewed, female biased sex ratio (Rania, et al., personal communication). Histological preparations revealed abnormalities in the differentiation of the gonadal tissue of many of these individuals. One hypothesis from this result is that some xenobiotic compounds may be affecting sexual differentiation in R. catesbeiana. We conducted two experiments to test this hypothesis. First, we treated larval R. catesbeiana with endosulfan, a locally sprayed pesticide that is known to be weakly estrogenic. We found significant differences in weight and mortality among 4 treatments (3 concentrations and a control) over a three week period. Next, we treated larval R. catesbeiana with zineb, a commonly used herbicide in the U.S. We found no statistical differences in weight or length among 5 treatments (4 concentrations and a control), although there were significant differences in mortality. These data suggest that larval bullfrogs exposed to pesticides may suffer deleterious effects.

title: Reef fishes from Parcel Manuel Luis Marine State Park, Maranhão, NE Brazil

abstract_text: The Parcel Manuel Luis Marine State Park (PEM), off Maranhão State, NE Brazil, is a large reef (18 km by 6 km) virtually unstudied biologically. Due to difficulty of access, a still unknown fish fauna is found in the area. This work is being developed in collaboration with the Maranhão State Environmental and Hydric Resources Bureau. Its main goals are to determine the composition and structure of the fish community, and to contribute to the management plan of the PEM. Data are being obtained through underwater observations, photographs and spear fishing. The method used to determine the community structure is the stationary visual census. In three expeditions (between August 1997 and January 1998) 103 species belonging to 47 families were recorded. The purple chromis, Chromis scotti, previously known only from the Caribbean and United States coast, was collected at PEM, where juveniles and adults were frequently seen close to the bottom in depths between 18 and 30m. Regarding the community structure, the herbivores most frequently seen, especially in the shallower areas, were Scarus coelestinus, Sparisoma viride and Kyphosus sectatrix. In the deeper areas (below 20m) the most common fishes were Chromis scotti, Gramma aff. loreto, and Halichoeres bivittatus.

title: Physiology and migratory behavior under different environmental conditions during the parr-smolt transformation of Atlantic salmon

abstract_text: Timing of physiological changes associated with the parr-smolt transformation has been intimately linked with changes in photoperiod and temperature. However, there is little direct evidence concerning environmental control of downstream migratory behavior. Seasonal timing of physiological and behavioral changes associated with increased temperatures was examined. Atlantic salmon parr and pre-smolts were tagged with passive integrated transponders (PIT) in March, placed in simulated stream conditions and monitored continuously from April through July. Water temperature was increased 1°C every 3 d (ambient), 1°C every other day (advanced), or 1°C every 9 d (delayed). The number of downstream passages of smolts peaked in May. Downstream movements of parr were two-orders of magnitude lower than of smolts. Fish maintained under ambient and advanced conditions ceased activity by mid-June. Fish exposed to the delayed temperature regime sustained downstream movements through July. In late June gill Na+, K+ -ATPase activity (an index of osmoregulatory physiology) had decreased in smolts maintained under ambient and advanced regimes, whereas it remained elevated in the delayed group. Temperature regimes dramatically affect smolt physiology, behavior, and migratory timing. Fluctuating water temperature and its influence on migration must be considered when contemplating survival of hatchery and wild smolts to the marine stage.

title: Declining temperature influences the osmoregulatory physiology of American shad, Alosa sapidissima, restricting the timing of seaward migration

abstract_text: Osmoregulatory abilities of American shad must be coordinated with migrations between fresh water (FW) and seawater (SW). Shad develop the ability to tolerate SW at larval-juvenile transition (26-45 d post-hatch) coincident with 3.5 and 10-fold increases in chloride cell (CC) number and gill Na+,K+-ATPase activity respectively. Although only early development is limited to low salinities, shad remain in FW for 5-6 months (until autumn). During autumnal migration juveniles lose the ability to osmoregulate in FW, evidenced by a decline in plasma chloride (20%). Shad kept in the laboratory through Dec. experience large declines in plasma chloride (68%) and high mortality. Gill Na+,K+-ATPase activity increases 3-fold and gill CC's on the primary and secondary lamellae increase 2-fold and 1.5-fold; these are likely to be compensatory mechanisms for increasing ion uptake. Changes in plasma chloride, gill Na+,K+-ATPase, and CC's are reduced and delayed if shad are maintained at 24°C versus a natural decline in temperature. Impaired osmoregulatory ability, as influenced by temperature, may serve as a proximate cue for migration. Changes in temperature (e.g. global warming) will likely alter the timing of migration.

title: Seasonally variable food availability constrains the timing of reproduction by herbivorous coral reef fishes

abstract_text: To date, few studies have examined how food availability may constrain the reproduction, growth and mortality of coral reef fishes in their natural habitat. To address this issue, we compared the life history tactics of supplementally fed, wild, adult beaugregory damselfish (Stegastes leucostictus) with those of control fish during a series of 90-day experimental trials. These herbivorous fish showed both seasonal and lunar patterns of reproduction in the study area off the coast of Panama. During the study, patterns of reproductive output and growth of control fish varied temporally and spatially, apparently in response to natural patterns of food availability. Growth rates, though variable, did not correspond well with levels of reproductive output. Mortality was generally high, though somewhat reduced during periods of low reproduction. Protein rich food supplements greatly increased reproduction and growth of experimental fish and substantially lowered rates of mortality, irrespective of season. These results strongly suggest that food limitation plays a critical role in determining both the seasonal timing and intensity of reproduction, growth, and mortality in this species.

title: Size-based delaying tactics in breeding schedule by brook trout: a removal experiment

abstract_text: Among salmonines (trout, salmon, char), there is a consistent trend for large females to spawn before small ones within a breeding season. This pattern may be related to competition for limited spawning sites or, alternatively, small females may delay reproduction as an adaptive tactic to minimise brood loss. Females routinely lose broods through the subsequent use of nest sites by other females. Broods of small females are more likely to be lost by this disturbance because nest depth is related to body size. We tested these alternative hypotheses by detaining the largest females in a marked population of lake-spawning brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis). The competition hypothesis predicts small females would breed earlier in the absence of large females, whereas the adaptive tactic hypothesis predicts delayed breeding. Consistent with our second hypothesis, small females spawned significantly later during the experimental year (1996) compared to the previous two years. Furthermore, brood loss was significantly reduced. Within seasons, brood loss was significantly higher for small than large females. Site choice may also play an important role in reproductive success. We show that small females increase reproductive success by delayed reproduction and suggest that this adaptive tactic may be socially mediated.

title: The effects of population structure on the timing of reproductive activity in male fathead minnows (Pimephales promelas): individual and population-level implications

abstract_text: Size-dependent asynchrony in the seasonal timing of reproduction has been well documented for fish in temperate regions. A common explanation of this phenomenon is that small fish are physiologically forced to postpone the allocation of energy to reproduction, resulting in a delay in the seasonal timing of reproductive activity. However, for male fathead minnows we suggest that the timing of seasonal reproductive activity is regulated by social interactions. In an enclosure and a pond experiment, small males advanced their reproductive condition, held nesting territories, and spawned only when isolated from large males or once large males were removed from the population. Small males were of similar size in all experimental treatments, suggesting that size-dependent differences in energy allocation do not account for differences in their phenology. Preliminary analyses also indicate that the production and size of young produced by small 'uninhibited' males was not significantly different from the production and size of young produced by large dominant males. Thus, the release of small males from social control may expedite population recovery following a size-dependent disturbance such as winterkill.

title: Seasonal aspects of resource allocation in Ambystoma opacum: implications for population dynamics

abstract_text: Marbled salamanders (Ambystoma opacum) inhabit woodlands throughout much of the eastern United States. Adults typically migrate to temporary pond breeding sites en masse in early autumn, where courtship, breeding, and terrestrial oviposition occur over a 3-4 week period. Energetically "spent" adults leave the site with virtually all lipid stores depleted. Experimental manipulations of food level suggest that adult reproductive frequency is dependent on prior food acquisition; thus food availability in the terrestrial habitat may partly explain the wide among-individual variation in year-to-year breeding patterns. Larval success is highly dependent on the timing of pond filling and drying: hydroperiod directly affects mortality and strongly influences competitive and predatory interactions. Per-capita food resources in the larval stage determine larval growth rates, larval period, body size at metamorphosis, and a suite of post-metamorphic adult traits. Although variation in larval period can be substantial, there is surprisingly little variation in the absolute date of metamorphosis. Larvae from eggs hatched 3-mo apart generally metamorphose within a few weeks of each other, regardless of whether the aquatic habitat remains suitable for growth. Later-hatching larvae therefore metamorphose at a smaller size in spite of the strong relationship between body size at metamorphosis and traits related to adult fitness. Food resources available to individuals in both the aquatic and terrestrial stages of the life cycle affect the resource allocation "decisions" a salamander makes. Understanding allocation decisions is critical to modeling the population dynamics of Ambystoma opacum.

title: Differential timing of maturation and reproduction in the salamander, Ambystoma talpoideum

abstract_text: Variation in abiotic parameters determines the timing of reproduction in many semi-aquatic amphibians; hence, the timing of first reproduction is constrained by extrinsic (e.g., temperature and rainfall) rather than intrinsic (e.g., the rate of gametogenesis) factors. Adaptations that release organisms from extrinsic factors may have important individual- and population-level implications. We describe the pattern of metamorphosis and maturation in natural and experimental populations of the salamander Ambystoma talpoideum. Prior to first reproduction (usually at 1-yr post-hatching), individuals that metamorphose are sexually immature when leaving the aquatic environment, and must mature in the terrestrial environment. Maturation, however, may precede metamorphosis. Individuals that mature prior to metamorphosis remain in the aquatic environment (i.e., become "paedomorphic"), are physiologically capable of breeding at the start of the breeding season, in the early fall. Terrestrial adults, however, must wait for the proper suite of environmental conditions to initiate migration to the aquatic breeding habitats, which may be delayed until mid to late winter. The result is a potentially large difference in the timing of reproduction between the two morphs. The consequences of differential maturation and reproduction among individuals may collectively have larger population-level effects.

abstract_text: Painted turtles (Chrysemys picta) hatch in late summer but usually remain in the nest during winter. Hatchlings can survive subzero temperatures in the nest either by tolerating the freezing of their body tissues, at temperatures to -4 °C, or by avoiding ice nucleation and remaining supercooled (unfrozen) to temperatures at least as low as -12 °C. We investigated the effects of soil composition and soil moisture on susceptibility to ice inoculation in hatchling turtles endemic to the sandhills of Nebraska, where soil moisture in winter is variable (range 4-14%). Turtles cooled in frozen, native soil (predominantly sand) froze at -1.6 °C, whereas turtles cooled in frozen soil to which clay or peat was added supercooled to -13 °C before freezing. Avoidance of inoculation by environmental ice in turtles exposed to frozen native soil was possible only when the soil contained little moisture (<4%). Thus, survival of relatively low nest temperatures, by supercooling, may be greater for turtles hibernating in sandy soils containing little moisture, or in soils containing clay or organic matter. However, the winter microenvironment contains numerous ice nuclei (e.g., inorganic particulates, microorganisms) that may nevertheless promote inoculative freezing.

abstract_text: Although studies of body temperature (Tb) are extensive for snakes living in temperate regions, few studies have focused on tropical, nocturnal snakes. title: Constraints on life histories of temperate-zone snakes: is the price of viviparity very high?

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Biology, University of Victoria, P.O. Box 3020 STN CSC, Victoria, B.C. V8W 3N5, Canada

abstract_text: In the highly seasonal environments of the north temperate zone, ectothermic animals such as snakes suffer significant temporal constraints on their annual cycles, with consequences for their life histories and demographies. For example, cold winters prohibit any activity at all, but summers also may be cool, further restricting activity. In presumed evolutionary response to this, most temperate-zone snakes are viviparous; gravid females exhibit precise behavioural thermoregulation, apparently providing optimal developmental conditions for their young. However, thermoregulation often conflicts with other activities such as feeding. In fact, in many species, gravid females feed little or not at all, even in captivity. The main demographic consequences of this are reduced future reproductive output, especially through decreased reproductive frequency of individual females. Nonetheless, this tradeoff may be relatively unimportant in the long run because many snakes are long-lived "bet-hedging" species and compensate for low reproductive output in one year by surviving to reproduce at a later date. I illustrate these ideas with data for garter snakes (Thamnophis) and rattlesnakes (Crotalus).

abstract_text: Among the most critically endangered sturgeon species worldwide are those in the genus Pseudoscaphirhynchus (Scaphirhynchinae), which are endemic to the Syr Darya (P. fedtschenkoi) and Amu Darya (P. kaufmanni and P. hermanni) rivers of the Aral Sea in central Asia. abstract_text: Studies on north temperate fish species indicate that new habitat availability following the last glacial retreat has promoted ecological speciation in post-glacial lakes. The extensive ecophenotypic polymorphism observed among Great Lakes ciscoes suggests that they have radiated through trophic adaptation and reproductive isolation. This study aims at relating the ecomorphological and genetic polymorphisms expressed by the Lake Nipigon ciscoes assemblage in order to evaluate the likelihood of an intralacustrine divergence driven by the exploitation of alternative resources. Morphological variation, trophic and spatial niche are characterized and contrasted among four putative species (N>200). Genetic variation at 10 microsatellite loci is analysed to appraise the extent of genetic structuring and reproductive isolation among species. Our results reveal various levels of niche overlap and indicate that Coregonus artedi is more generalist than C. nigripinnis, C. hoyi and C. zenethicus. title: Phylogeny and biogeography of ricefishes (Beloniformes, Adrianichthyidae)

abstract_text: Ricefishes, known best by the medaka, Oryzias latipes, are classified in the family Adrianichthyidae in the atherinomorph order Beloniformes. The approximately twenty-five ricefish species range throughout fresh and brackish waters of eastern Eurasia, Southeast Asia, the Indian subcontinent, across the Indo-Australian archipelago, crossing Wallace's Line, to Timor. Throughout most of their range, ricefishes are small, reaching about 40 mm SL; in the tectonic lakes of Sulawesi, however, ricefishes are relative giants, reaching about 200 mm SL. Ricefishes are monophyletic and comprise two monophyletic subgroups or lineages, one large bodied and one small, diagnosed here by morphological characters. Outgroup comparison using traditional morphology supports a transformation from large to small, whereas preliminary molecular data supports a transformation from small to large. Sulawesi ricefishes are not monophyletic but, instead, include members of each of the two lineages. As expected, the sister taxa have an area of overlap, or sympatry, in Sulawesi. This distribution pattern is found in other fish taxa, supporting the idea that neither lineage is primitive to the other, but that there was a widespread ancestral taxon, and, once sister lineages diverged, some members of one or both lineages dispersed into the range of the other.
